name: Opus Broadening
strategy: Broadening expressed outside the US index-structure trade: long international developed and emerging markets, the physical AI/defense capex complex, large-cap value, insurance and power, funded against a short of the crowded US momentum factor.
reassessment_note: I am replacing this book outright, and the reason is that the previous leg was not a broadening book at all - it was a long-crowded-momentum book wearing my name. Long FTNT, PANW, NET, SNOW, TWLO, MU, XYZ with a short of ORCL is the single most concentrated factor bet available in US equities, and this week it did exactly what crowded momentum does when the regime shifts: PANW -12.8% after fiscal Q4 next-gen security ARR came in light of buy-side expectations, NET -8.6%, FTNT -8.6%, and the whole book at -3.75% NAV against SPY +3.62%. Two things now make holding it indefensible. First, the macro: 162k August payrolls versus 53k expected, unemployment steady at 4.1%, the 2-year at 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year at 4.78%, and futures pricing roughly 53-65% odds of a rate HIKE on September 15-16 with August CPI on 9/11 as the trigger - high-multiple software is the worst-positioned asset class in the market for a hawkish surprise. Second, the specific: my ORCL short (already -6.5% against me) sits directly in front of Oracle's fiscal Q1 2027 report on September 10, a binary AI-backlog event I have no edge on and no business holding a short into. So the replacement goes back to the mandate. Broadening is not only 'equal-weight beats cap-weight' - that is what my Round 2 book already owns. The second, genuinely different expression is broadening across geographies and into the physical economy: international developed and EM equity, infrastructure and aerospace/defense capex, large-cap value, insurance (which earns rather than suffers from a higher front end), and power demand, with the crowded US momentum factor sold short via MTUM as the direct anti-concentration leg. Ticker overlap with my Round 2 book is zero and same-direction overlap is far under the 50% novelty limit: R2 owns US equal-weight, small/mid caps, energy, materials, banks, biotech and an ETH tail short QQQ; this book owns none of those. Cash is lifted to 18% at 4% APY as dry powder across the 9/11 CPI and the 9/16 FOMC.

positions.thesis: The largest leg, and the most literal reading of the mandate: broadening does not stop at the US border. Developed ex-US equity is the deepest pool of the market that is not the Mag 7 - Europe and Japan large-caps trade at a persistent multiple discount with far less index concentration than the S&P, so a world where leadership disperses is a world where they re-rate. The honest risk is the dollar, which firmed on Friday's hawkish reset and would firm further on a September hike, translating foreign returns down; that is why this is 13% rather than 20% and why it carries a 12% stop. I take that risk because dollar strength driven by US rate differentials tends to be the thing that mean-reverts once the hike is actually delivered.

The physical AI trade rather than the software AI trade, at $55.16 after a 21% trailing year. Everything the market is paying enormous multiples for in semis and software has to be poured, wired and energized first: grid capacity, transmission, datacenter construction, electrical equipment, engineering and construction. Industrials were one of only three winning sectors on Friday's hawkish tape and copper rose 1.95% on the week, which is the tape confirming the demand is physical and current. It is also structurally the right leg for this regime - these companies earn on nominal capex budgets rather than on a discount rate, so a hike hurts them far less than it hurts the software names this book just sold. 30% take-profit because this is a theme that can run hard and I want a discipline for taking it.

Large-cap value is the other 493 companies in one instrument, and it is the cleanest way to own broadening within US large-caps without duplicating my Round 2 equal-weight core. The 2026 evidence is that this is working - Mag 7 flat in the first half against +9.3% for the S&P, with heavy AI capital spending now weighing on sentiment toward the very names that led for three years. Value's low duration is also the right shape for a market pricing a 50-65% chance of a hike: financials, healthcare, staples and energy weights earn near-term cash flows that a higher discount rate barely touches. 12% at a 12% stop makes this a core sleeve rather than a satellite.

Aerospace and defense is breadth with a funding source that does not care about the Fed. Defense budgets and the commercial aerospace delivery backlog are multi-year appropriations and order books, so the earnings stream is about as insulated from a September rate decision as an equity sleeve gets, and defense sits alongside grid and AI infrastructure in the capital-spending cycle that is currently driving industrials leadership. It is genuinely uncorrelated with everything in my Round 2 book, which is exactly what a second expression of the mandate should add. 10% with a 14% stop and a 30% take-profit.

Insurance is my direct beneficiary of the hawkish repricing, and it is deliberately not the bank version of that trade - my Round 2 book already owns KRE, and insurers carry none of the deposit-flight or commercial real estate credit exposure that makes regional banks gap. With the 2-year at 4.37%, the highest since January 2025, insurers reinvest float at yields they have not seen in nearly two years, and property and casualty pricing remains firm. If the Fed actually hikes on September 16, this is the leg that goes up on the news. 8% with a 13% stop.

The anti-concentration leg, and the intellectual core of this replacement. MTUM at $304.86 is up 26.5% over the trailing year and mechanically owns whatever has already worked - which right now is the same crowded software and AI complex whose cracks I just watched break my previous book. Shorting the momentum factor is the precise expression of a broadening thesis: I get paid when leadership disperses, and I get paid specifically in the scenario that hurt me last week rather than being run over by it again. It is a different instrument and a different exposure from the QQQ short in my Round 2 book - a factor short, not a mega-cap index short. Held at 8% and no larger because shorting a rising factor is a hedge with a 3% borrow cost, not a conviction bet; 10% stop, 20% take-profit.

Utilities were one of the three winning sectors on Friday's hawkish tape, which is unusual and informative - a bond proxy that rallies as the 2-year hits a 20-month high is being bought for its earnings, not its yield. That earnings story is datacenter and electrification load growth, the demand side of the same AI buildout PAVE supplies. I keep it a modest 7% precisely because the rate sensitivity is real and a hike could reassert itself over the load-growth narrative, but a broadening book that owns the power demand behind AI without owning AI multiples is doing its job. 12% stop.

Emerging markets are the highest-beta version of the geographic broadening this book is built on, sized small at 6% because they carry the sharpest version of its main risk: a firmer dollar on hawkish Fed repricing tightens EM financial conditions directly. The offset is that EM earnings are levered to the commodity and capex cycle that is visibly live - copper +1.95% and WTI +9.5% on the week - and EM sits at a valuation discount that makes it the natural destination for money leaving US mega-cap concentration. A satellite position with a wide 15% stop, sized so that being early costs the book under a percent.

Japan as a distinct sleeve rather than being buried inside VEA, because the driver is idiosyncratic: the corporate governance and capital-return reform cycle, buybacks and cross-shareholding unwinds, plus the domestic reflation that finally lets Japanese banks and industrials earn a spread. Its correlation to a US Fed decision is the loosest of any equity leg in the book, which is what I want alongside a 9/11 CPI and a 9/16 FOMC. A deliberate 6% satellite - conviction in the structural story, respect for the fact that a stronger dollar and a hawkish BOJ response can both move against it. 12% stop.
